item.title: Beyond the Ligand Applicability Domain: Generalization and Local Resolution in Structure-Aware Foundation Models for Affinity Prediction
item.description: Structure-aware foundation models that jointly represent proteins and ligands promise to extend affinity prediction beyond the chemical applicability domains of conventional ligand-based models, but whether they provide sufficient resolution to guide fine-grained medicinal-chemistry decisions remains unclear. We evaluatedBoltz-2across12kinasetargetsusinghistoricalbioactivityreconstruction,binding-pocket randomization, cross-target selectivity analysis, and chemical-series evaluation. Across chemically diverse compounds in temporally reconstructed evaluation sets, Boltz-2 and target-specific ligand-based machine learningshowedcomparablemeanglobalrankingacrosstargets,withsubstantialtarget-dependent differences (mean Kendall’s τ = 0.40 vs 0.31). Randomizing the binding pocket reduced mean τ from 0.33 to 0.14, while predictions were centered near −7.64 kcal/mol and retained correlated compound profiles acrossproteins.Together,theseresultssuggestastrongligand-conditionedsignal,withadditional predictive information contributed by the protein pocket. Despite this protein sensitivity, compound-level selectivitypredictionremainedweak(meanτ=0.17),andtheexperimentallystrongesttargetwas recovered for only 18.9% of compounds. Ranking also weakened within 72 temporally classified chemical series and varied substantially among series (protein-balanced mean τ = 0.18 for Boltz-2 and 0.09 for ligand-based models). These results show that structure-aware models can recover affinity information beyond relationshipscaptured by conventionalligand-based approaches whilerevealingaresolution boundary between broad prioritization and the local energetic discrimination required for selectivity and analogue ranking. At their current demonstrated resolution, such models appear best suited to broad compound or series prioritization and complementary hypothesis generation. Extending their use to fine analogueranking,selectivityoptimization,andinterpretationofsmallaffinitydifferenceswillrequire prospective evidence of reliable local resolution.

item.title: SMILES serialization changes activity-cliff annotations in the MoleculeACE benchmark
item.description: MoleculeACE is a widely used benchmark that annotates activity-cliff compounds in 30 ChEMBL datasets and reports that machine-learning models predict them poorly. Its “soft consensus” criterion admits a compound pair when any of three similarities reaches 0.9: ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity, Tanimoto similarity of anonymized molecular graphs, or normalized Levenshtein similarity between SMILES strings. The first two are computed after parsing; the third operates on the supplied strings, which the benchmark code does not canonicalize. This study held molecules, potencies, thresholds and code fixed and varied only how the same molecules werewritten. A re-implementation reproduced the distributed labels exactly in 27 of 30 datasets, and canonical round-tripping changed amedian of 0.00% of labels. Re-serializing themolecules with two independent cheminformatics toolkits, with every rewritten string verified to encode the original molecule, changed a median of 8.98% (Indigo) and 9.48% (Open Babel) of compound labels; Kekulé SMILES from RDKit changed 5.23%, and randomized SMILES 17.05%. The graph-derived criteria were invariant across all rewrites. Because MoleculeACE stratifies its train/test split on the cliff label, changing the labels caused split membership to approach that of an independent redraw (31.3% of compounds reassigned, against a 32.21% ceiling). An end-to-end repair, with serialization-invariant labels, re-derived splits and retrained descriptorbased models, moved the pooled cliff penalty by −0.006 to +0.020 log units; every confidence interval included zero against a minimum detectable effect of 0.041–0.057, and for SVM the shift fell within the variability of same-definition split redraws of comparable magnitude. The distributed annotation is therefore reproducible but not invariant to valid serialization. Benchmarks that retain string-based criteria should specify and enforce the canonicalization contract (toolkit, version and output mode); otherwise, labels should be defined on parsed molecular representations. Serialization-invariant labels, splits and per-molecule predictions are released.

item.title: Raman Spectroscopy Reveals Isotope-specific Hydrogen Bond Kinetics in a Spherical Droplet leading to Preferential Evaporation of D2O in H2O-D2O Mixture
item.description: The evaporation of a spherical droplet having a pure solvent or a mixture of isotopic forms is fundamental to atmospheric physics, and critical for studying interfacial fluid dynamics, and hydrogen-bond kinetics. Understanding the hydrogen/deuterium bonded structural dynamics at molecular level during evaporation of isotopic water mixture (H2O/D2O) is important for understanding non-equilibrium phase transitions. In this work, we investigated real-time evaporation kinetics of spherical water droplets on superhydrophobic surface by time - dependent Raman spectroscopic method. Specifically, the results give an account for the variation of each H - or D-bonded clusters (ranging from fully tetrahedral ice-like structure to free water molecule) with time in the mixture from the time - dependent intensity change of each distinct vibrational stretching band of O-H or O-D. For pure H2O, the O-H peak intensities for all the clusters were decreasing with time, whereas for pure D2O, the ice-like structures vanished quickly with simultaneous increase in the free D2O molecules. In the mixture of H2O-D2O, based on Raman signal of each species, our experimental measurements suggested that the species having O-D or D2O was evaporating faster in comparison to the species having O-H or H2O. The results were also supported by the molecular dynamics simulation, which revealed that the bulk D2O was moving to the surface, and evaporating faster than H2O molecules.

item.title: A Biobased Epoxy Resin with Sequential Thermoplastic-to-Thermoset Curing Enables Removable-to-Permanent Adhesive Bonding
item.description: Adhesives are commonly designed either as reworkable thermoplastics or permanently crosslinked thermosets. Here, sequential thermoplastic-to-thermoset curing enables a simple two-component formulation based on a bio-based epoxy resin to function first as a removable hot-melt adhesive and subsequently as a permanent structural adhesive. Reaction of diglycidyl ether of vanillyl alcohol (DGEVA) and anilinium methanesulfonate at 110 °C produces a thermoplastic intermediate that is solid at room temperature but flows upon reheating and dissolves in selected solvents. This intermediate forms load-bearing joints that can be thermally debonded and rebonded or disassembled by dissolution. Further heating induces crosslinking and converts the same adhesive layer into a permanent epoxy network, increasing the apparent lap-shear strength nearly eightfold and rendering the joint resistant to disassembly under the same solvent conditions. This curing sequence therefore assigns reworkability and high-strength permanent bonding to successive adhesive states within the same formulation.

item.title: On how cell shape determines bactericidal effects of nanopatterned surfaces
item.description: Nanopatterned surfaces inactivate bacteria by mechanically deforming adherent cells, yet design guidelines remain inconsistent and studies rarely isolate the role of cell shape. Here, we show how cell shape governs responses to nanopatterned surfaces. We develop a thermodynamic model coupling envelope stretching and bending with cell-surface adhesion to compare spherical and rod-shaped bacteria with identical cross-sections. We find that nanopatterning increases strain for both shapes, while cell shape changes how cells attain that strain. We show that spherical and rod-shaped cells adopt different adhesion geometries and energy balances even when they experience similar strains. Rod-shaped cells reach higher strains at lower nanopillar densities over much of the design space, while nanopillar radius and density tune cell shape-dependent strain differences. We identify nanopatterns that preferentially strain either shape or balance their responses using Pareto analysis. Together, our results establish cell shape as a key design consideration for tailoring bactericidal nanopatterned materials.

item.title: Synthetic Methodologies to Access Fused Six-Membered Phosphorus Heterocycles
item.description: π-Conjugated molecules are essential in a wide range of modern technologies: organic electronics, sensing and biomedical applications. The incorporation of heteroatoms into fused aromatic systems represents a key strategy to modulate their optoelectronic properties. While nitrogen, sulfur and oxygen have been extensively investigated in this context, phosphorus remains far less explored, despite offering a unique combination of properties: tunable oxidation states, rich coordination chemistry, non-planar geometry at heterocyclic rings, and a strong ability to lower the LUMO energy of π-systems. These properties make six-membered phosphorus heterocycles especially attractive building blocks with capabilities that other heteroatoms simply cannot provide. However, the synthetic methodologies available to incorporate these heterocycles into large fused π-conjugated architectures remain underdeveloped, hampering broader exploration of their extraordinary potential. In this review, we aim to offer synthetic and organometallic chemists a starting point to identify current limitations and develop new, more versatile strategies for incorporating these heterocycles into fused architectures, and, in turn, a practical guide for materials scientists seeking to design new π-extended phosphorus systems. In particular, we provide a systematic catalog of the cyclization reactions reported to date for the preparation of six-membered phosphorus heterocycles fused at different positions to aromatic rings, organized around five model structures according to the bond(s) at which fusion takes place, from metal-free strategies to the transition-metal-mediated C-P bond-forming methodologies that have driven much of the recent progress. We anticipate that this overview will encourage new, more efficient synthetic routes to fused phosphorus heterocycles, broadening access to this underexploited class of π-extended systems.

item.title: Electronic Structure, Bonding Topology, and Photophysical Properties of the Low-Valent Beryllium Cluster CpBe2NO: A Multireference and Real-Space Wavefunction Analysis
item.description: A comprehensive ab initio investigation of the cyclopentadienyl-beryllium nitrosyl complex (CpBe2NO) was conducted using complete active space self-consistent field (CASSCF), strongly contracted n-electron valence state perturbation theory (SC-NEVPT2), complete active space second-order perturbation theory (CASPT2), and symmetry-adapted cluster/similarity transformed equation-of-motion domain-based local pair-natural orbital coupled-cluster (STEOM-DLPNO-CCSD) methods, in conjunction with quantum theory of atoms in molecules (QTAIM) and real-space wavefunction topology analyses. The singlet–triplet energy gap indicates a triplet ground state at the CASSCF level. Relaxed CASPT2 potential energy surface scans along the Be–Be internuclear coordinate establish an equilibrium singlet bond distance of 2.200 Å, a dissociation energy (De) of 21.11 kcal mol-1, and a harmonic vibrational frequency (ωe) of 593.75 cm-1. Active-space natural orbital populations and QTAIM bond critical point (BCP) decompositions demonstrate pronounced multireference character and multi-center metallic bonding. STEOM-DLPNO-CCSD excited-state calculations map vertical transition energies, oscillator strengths, and unrelaxed dipole moments across the low-lying singlet manifold. Real-space descriptors—including the electron localization function (ELF), localized orbital locator (LOL), reduced density gradient (RDG), and interaction region indicator (IRI)—further elucidate the electronic shell structure and attractive metallic interaction basins.

item.title: Provenance-Aware Quality Control for Heterogeneous Bioactivity Data
item.description: Background. Machine-learning models for proteins increasingly train on large, pooled collections of laboratory measurements-binding affinities such as IC50, Ki, Kd and EC50 (numbers that describe how tightly a molecule binds its target), togetherwith biophysical readouts from techniques such as surface plasmon resonance (SPR), bio-layer interferometry (BLI) and isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). These measurements arrive in different units, from different assay formats, fitted with different models, and at different levels of quality. Pooling them without care injects substantial noise. The per-record quality flags that some databases attach are incomplete, and they do not travel with the data once records from several sources are combined. What has been missing is an open, model-agnostic layer that turns raw measurements into records a downstream pipeline can consume directly: unit-normalized, quality-checked, and carrying their own uncertainty and provenance. What we built. biophys_interop is an open Python toolkit and data schema. It maps any supportedmeasurement to a single canonical record spanning 24 measurement types (modalities), converts units to a common standard, and runs a registry of 72 deterministic, method-aware quality-control (QC) rules. Every rule cites a reason from the measurement literature, recommends a concrete action, and returns a simple pass / warn / fail flag together with a calibrated uncertainty. The library is small and has few dependencies. We are deliberate about what our validation does and does not cover: two broadly applicable affinity rules (a plausible-value-range rule and an exact-duplicate rule) are tested at scale against an independent curator’s labels; the remaining method-specific biophysical rules are offered as a literaturegrounded, executable registry-useful and auditable, but not claimed as validated here, because no public database publishes the per-record ground-truth flags that would be needed to score them. Results. Using ChEMBL’s own data_validity_comment and potential_duplicate annotations as an independent ground truth, transparent rules on the standardized record reproduce two of ChEMBL’s three curator flag families on 175,387 held-out records across 30 human targets, with no trained model (value-range rule: Matthews correlation coefficient [MCC] 0.61; duplicate rule: MCC 0.65). The thresholds transfer cleanly to a completely separate set of targets (train on 15, test on 15 disjoint targets; 88,443 held-out records; MCC 0.73 and 0.64). Going beyond the curator, the layer flags 929 internally inconsistent records that ChEMBL did not flag, and a comparison against the independent BindingDB database exposes 38 disagreements of 100-fold or more, 89% of them unmarked by either database. A domain expert who checked a 24-record sample against the primary literature confirmed 16 of 24 (67%) as genuine data errors, including 11 of 12 cross-database conflicts. We reproduce the known cross-assay noise regime reported by Landrum and Riniker, and show that a comparability gate based on assay metadata more than halves the median disagreement between records (0.51-> 0.21 log units). Finally, feeding the calibrated signal into a downstreammutation-effect (ΔΔG) predictor gave no reliable improvement; we report this negative result in full. The toolkit, the rule registry, the cleaned datasets, and one-command reproduction scripts are released openly. Conclusions. Once heterogeneous public measurements share one representation, simple transparent rules can catch data problems-matching expert curators at scale on the rule families we tested, and catching errors those curators missed. The result is a reusable, auditable data layer for protein machine learning, rather than a new predictive model. Keywords: bioactivity data; data curation; quality control; ChEMBL; BindingDB; data standardization; FAIR data; machine learning; interoperability; reproducibility

item.title: Hybrid-CatBoost: an empirical comparison of molecular representations for aqueous-solubility prediction on the TDC benchmark
item.description: Aqueous-solubility prediction depends on both molecular representation and the definition of the target. We compared fingerprint, descriptor, hybrid, and graph-based representations on the TDC Solubility_AqSolDB benchmark using five official scaffold splits and a fixed test set of 1,997 records. Hybrid-CatBoost achieved a five-run test MAE of 0.749631 ± 0.016216 TDC logS units, compared with 0.764558 ± 0.009666 for descriptor-only CatBoost. However, the corresponding validation improvement was small (ΔMAE = −0.004932) and occurred in only two of five matched splits. Errors increased toward both target extremes and showed opposite-signed residual biases. These results indicate that descriptor-based models capture most of the predictive signal in this benchmark, while the added Morgan fingerprint provides only a modest and split-dependent benefit. Interpretation is limited by incomplete assay metadata and the use of a single fixed test set, which does not provide external validation.

item.title: Electrochemical passivation of LiFePO4 cathodes by polaron crystallization during cell cycling
item.description: The nature of intermediate phases during LiFePO4 cycling and their role in limiting lithium transport remain unresolved. Building on our pioneering application of operando 57Fe nuclear resonance vibrational spectroscopy to working batteries, we combine this element-specific probe with machine-learning-based spectral analysis to resolve and quantify a vibrational signature of an intermediate component distinct from the LiFePO4 and FePO4 end-members. Its maximum molar fraction reaches nearly 20% at cycling rates of C/10, C/5 and C/2, revealing a rateindependent formation of intermediate phase. The intermediate exhibits additional distinct feature in the Fe-projected phonon density of states, suggesting localized Fe3+ hole-polaron environments, which is supported by atomistic simulations. These observations motivate a working hypothesis linking the persistence of the intermediate to restricted lithium transport. We propose that local accumulation of hole polarons along with elastic stress at phase interface promotes their crystallization into an ordered superstructure at the advancing phase boundary. Ordering restricts polaron motion and through lithium ion–polaron coupling reduces lithium-ion mobility across the intermediate layer. This layer could therefore to certain extent passivate individual particles against further delithiation, allowing transformation to proceed elsewhere in the electrode. The proposed mechanism offers an explanation for the nearly rate-independent intermediate phase fraction and identifies polaron ordering as a potential target for improving high-rate performance, for example through dopants that inhibit polaron crystallization.

item.title: Computational shielding of chikungunya viral prefusion with permeable cyclic-minipeptides
item.description: Permeable cyclic-minipeptide-conformer candidates were computationally co-generated with the aim of shielding the protected prefusion-loops (FL) of the envelop E2E1 protein heterodimers of chikungunya virus (CHIKV). This work attempts to prevent some of the earliest pH-dependent dissociation E2E1 events which trigger CHIKV fusion/ infectivity by fully exposing their FL. To co-generate de novo candidates, a minimized prefusion CHIKV E2E1 (minE2E1) model including minimal E2-protective and E1-FL sequences was targeted by BoltzGen. The advantages of the cogenerated top-affinity nanoMolar candidates include higher affinities compared to previous neutralizing peptides, easier chemical synthesis, low antigenicity and strong conformer stabilities. Top-affinity parents were computationally mutated to derive thousands of membrane-permeable candidates conserving their cyclization, targets and affinities. A few membrane-permeable top-affinity candidates may serve for experimentally-guided validation of possible inhibition of CHIKV fusion and infection.

item.title: Computational assessment, against criteria specified in advance, of a Na+/Ag+ ion-exchange route to Ag2MgSiO4, a predicted wurtzite-derived silver silicate
item.description: Many metastable inorganic compounds exist only because a synthetic route delivers them, and database screening is poorly placed to find them. Topotactic ion exchange is such a route: at low temperature it swaps the mobile cation of a known parent for another, ideally while the framework stays intact, yet it is rarely assessed computationally before synthesis. We test whether a simple exchange-energy criterion, specified in advance and checked against independent calculations, can nominate a credible target. Computed with a machine-learned interatomic potential, the criterion reproduced the sign of 42 published DFT exchange enthalpies (36/36 for |∆H| ≥ 10 kJ mol−1) and selected Ag2MgSiO4, to be made from Na2MgSiO4 in molten AgNO3. Density functional theory gives an exchange energy of about −58 kJ mol−1 per Ag, within the ±10 kJ mol−1 window around three reported preparations of silver silicates and germanates from sodium parents in molten AgNO3, and an energy above the hull (0.038–0.042 eV atom−1) like that of known silver silicates. The Pna21 structure is dynamically stable in the harmonic approximation (0 K). Calculated Ag+ hop barriers are comparable to or lower than those of a reported Ag+ conductor, and the HSE06 gap, calibrated on one literature value, is about 3 eV, at the violet edge of the visible range. These are 0 K predictions; no synthesis was attempted, and the closest precedent is Ag2MnSiO4, so a single exchange experiment can confirm or refute them (incomplete exchange or changes in particle size and shape are reported in some precedents).

item.title: Machine Learning-Powered Simulations of Confinement-Driven 129Xe Nuclear Spin Relaxation
item.description: The rate at which a nuclear spin returns to equilibrium encodes the dynamics of its surroundings, information the chemical shift, a time-averaged quantity, cannot provide. Building on a previous dual-model machine learning framework, combining a fine-tuned atomistic foundation model (FT-AFM) for molecular dynamics (MD) with an NMR-ML model predicting the 129Xe magnetic shielding tensor, we compute the chemical shift anisotropy-driven 129Xe spin-lattice (T1) and spin-spin (T2) relaxation times of xenon confined in carbon nanotubes by extending the Redfield theory treatment to arbitrary nanotube orientations relative to the external magnetic field. Across various temperatures, nanotube diameters, and Xe loadings, both relaxation times evolve non-monotonically in several cases, and for systems whose Xe densities match those of experimental free xenon gas, confinement shortens T1 by up to fivefold. We also show that T1 provides an indirect NMR probe of single-file Xe diffusion. This work establishes FT-AFMs and NMR-ML models as a fast, accurate, and general route to the nuclear spin relaxation of confined Xe across a broad range of porous materials.

item.title: Magnetic control of lipid–peroxyl termination yield under spin relaxation: from an optimised dipolar-scale field to a falsifiable kinetic criterion
item.description: Lipid peroxidation, the radical-chain oxidation of membrane lipids, terminates in part through spin-selective encounters between lipid-peroxyl radicals. We ask how far a shaped magnetic field can steer this branch under spin relaxation and how that change propagates to the oxidation flux. Gradient-projection and bang–bang Pontryagin controls were evaluated with a stochastic-Schrödinger treatment of dipolar fluctuations and an independent Brownian-dynamics model. A best-found dipolar-scale field raises the triplet-initialised singlet termination yield from ΦS|T = 0.220 at 50 µT to 0.562 (+155%), with the bang–bang solution corroborating at 0.522; a bandwidth-filtered proxy retains 0.270. Under Brownian dynamics the control advantage remains positive throughout the sampled rotational-correlation-time range, and one field transfers across eight microdomain-size–diffusion parameter sets. Closing the spin calculation to classical autoxidation kinetics gives Ceff = −f/(1+f), where f is the fraction of peroxyl loss proceeding through bimolecular termination. Two limiting descriptions of the productive encounter population bracket the predicted suppression of oxidation flux in antioxidant-free liposomes at approximately 21–37%, and at approximately 4–10% for the bandwidth-filtered field. α-Tocopherol attenuates the response as interception comes to dominate, providing an internal experimental control. These values describe an elementary encounter and a minimal kinetic model, not whole-cell lipid peroxidation.

item.title: TiO2 as active site and protective layer on Sn doped spinel cobalt oxide for acidic OER

item.title: Multiscale Insights into CO2 Chemisorption and Proton Transfer in Choline-Imidazolate based Deep Eutectic solvents: Exploring the Effect of Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Alkanolamine on Reaction Pathways and Product Distribution
item.description: Understanding how solvent composition governs competitive CO2 chemisorption within solvents is essential for the rational design of solvents for CO2 capture. In this work, we combine density functional theory (DFT), classical molecular dynamics (cMD), and microkinetic modeling to investigate CO2 chemisorption in choline-imidazolate based systems containing different alkanolamine hydrogen bond donors (HBDs): monoethanolamine (MEA), diethanolamine (DEA), and methyldiethanolamine (MDEA). By systematically characterizing the thermodynamics, kinetics and liquid structure influence, our results show that within these systems, choline is the preferred CO2-binding site unless a HBD is present. Accordingly, the MEA system shifts almost entirely to amine-centered carbamate formation, the DEA system retains carbamate dominance but with stronger competition from choline-centered capture, and the MDEA system which additionally includes water shifts back toward choline-centered carbonate together with a competitive water-assisted bicarbonate pathway. The findings illustrate how CO2 chemisorption in multicomponent liquids is controlled by a combination of intrinsic reaction thermodynamics, liquid-structure, and CO2 concentration. More broadly, this work provides insights that will facilitate molecular-level design of solvents for CO2 uptake and regeneration.

item.title: Talking to instruments: device-integration standards for self-driving laboratories
item.description: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are rapidly outgrowing the single-instrument prototype, scaling into multi-instrument and multi-site platforms that run autonomous discovery across chemistry, materials science, biotechnology, pharmaceutical re-search and adjacent domains. What now decides whether an SDL can scale, share its integrations and federate experiments is no longer the algorithms or the robots, but the software layer that orchestrates heterogeneous devices. Today that layer is the bottleneck: a fast-growing ecosystem of open-source orchestrators in which most have built device integration on their own bespoke conventions instead of adopting a formally governed standard. The result is predictable and costly. Integrations do not transfer between laboratories, orchestrators cannot interoperate and many new SDLs rebuild their device-control layer from scratch.
